en_title: 2. Mental Health and Immigration: What Nobody Tells You
en_excerpt: What almost nobody tells you about moving abroad: the anxiety, loneliness and pressure that arrive along with the suitcases — and where to find help in Ireland.
en_meta_description: Anxiety, loneliness and depression among immigrants in Ireland — the warning signs, and where to find support in Portuguese or English.
en_content:
Text: Lili Fraga –

Therapist and Parent Educator

Central theme: Anxiety, loneliness and depression among immigrants

Talking about the emotional impact of starting over in another country, the pressure to succeed, and how to find help (in Portuguese or English) in Ireland. Including warning signs and paths to support.

🧠 Mental Health and Immigration: What Nobody Tells You

Anxiety, loneliness and depression far from home

Have you ever heard that phrase “Just come!” when someone talks about living abroad, doing a study exchange or moving to another country? Well… it sounds like a light invitation, full of promises — freedom, opportunities, money, quality of life. But what almost nobody tells you is that, along with the suitcases, come the doubts, the pressures, the longing and, often, the emotional silence.

Sometimes the desire to change is so intense that we set off without looking deeply into our inner possibilities. We lack the time (or the courage) to ask ourselves: “Am I ready for this fresh start?” Because yes, living abroad is a transformative experience — but it demands an immense emotional maturity.

Worries are not limited to housing or work. They invade your sleep, your mood, your vital energy. Starting over, reinventing yourself and, above all, finding yourself are key pieces so that you do not lose yourself along the way.

Living abroad demands emotional planning and deep listening:

●      What are my limits?

●      How do I deal with frustrations?

●      Am I willing to live the new without cancelling who I am?

And this is where the central point of this conversation comes in: mental health in immigration.

🔍 The psychological impact of starting over

Studies indicate that immigrants show higher rates of anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress than local populations. This happens for several reasons: social isolation, language difficulties, culture shock, financial insecurity and lack of a support network (FERREIRA, Alisson Vinícius Silva; BORGES, Lucienne Martins, 2022; WHO, 2018).

In Ireland, a study with Brazilians revealed that many live with significant levels of stress, especially women and mothers who feel overwhelmed because they are the pillar of the family while facing cultural and language barriers (Ribeiro et al., 2020).

⚠️ Warning signs

Noticing that something is wrong is not always easy. But pay attention to a few signs:

●      Difficulty sleeping or waking up rested

●      Constant irritability or crying spells with no apparent reason

●      Lack of motivation, loss of pleasure in simple things

●      Self-deprecating thoughts or a feeling of inadequacy

●      A feeling of loneliness even when surrounded by people

●      Intense anxiety in the face of ordinary tasks (going to the shop, talking to someone, leaving the house)

These symptoms are not weakness. They are requests for help.

🧭 Paths to support

If you recognised yourself in any of these situations, know that you are not alone — and you do not have to face this without support. Here in Ireland there are resources available, both in Portuguese and in English:

🌿 Support in Portuguese:

●      Jigsaw (Wellbeing for Young Adults) – although it operates in English, it offers support for young adults and usually has interpreters available.

https://jigsaw.ie/talk-online/live-chat/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=10646051693&gbraid=0AAAAADgoh_Lkn3GQPGrOmaEOHaAC2Hl7P&gclid=Cj0KCQjw5c_FBhDJARIsAIcmHK-LcSCQsv64GoMKCmZ-BnUqx6yxZ–9UbybKLXHbkkEg7lk_guxdUQaAvmKEALw_wcB

●      Dublin Community Support Groups – there are informal groups of Brazilians and therapists working online.  

https://grow.ie/category/recovery-stories/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=13611074611&gbraid=0AAAAADmGKBwtsy7WFEb3_AayfRM2ZjC-3&gclid=Cj0KCQjw5c_FBhDJARIsAIcmHK8KnYFNNnYedcAMITdkJXl6XuRxYITttshrEEljeJHZrbuRBdjC2MgaAsR8EALw_wcB

🌱 Support in English:

●      Mental Health Ireland https://www.mentalhealthireland.ie/ 

●      Samaritans (free 24-hour helpline: 116 123)

●      MyMind.ie – offers psychotherapy sessions at affordable prices (often with therapists who speak Portuguese) https://mymind.org/ 

💛 Wrapping up…

Dealing with mental health in immigration is an act of courage. It means stepping out of denial and saying: “I matter. My feelings are valid. And I deserve support.”

You do not have to be fine all the time. But you can aim to be fine with yourself, even on difficult days.

🗓️ Next month, we will talk about the power of support networks in the life of an immigrant:

 “Building a Support Network Far From Home”. Because nobody has to walk this path alone — and when we walk together, everything feels lighter.

With affection, Lili Fraga – Therapist and Parent Educator http://www.instagram.com/lilifraga.vivaleve
